entry.title: Langevin diffusion
entry.content:
Recall that a stochastic process $X_t$ is called a diffusion process if it satisfies

\[ egin{aligned} dX_t = \mu(t, X_t)dt + \sigma(t, X_t)dW_t. \end{aligned}\]

In other words, from the Markov property, the movement of the stochastic process only depends on the time $t$ and its current location. In particular, we study time-homogeneous processes, in which the functions $\mu$ and $\sigma$ do not depend on $t$ [Chewi, Log-concave sampling].

Definition. Let $V: \mathbb R^d o \mathbb R$ be a potential in $C^2$ and strongly convex function. The Langevin diffusion is the stochastic process taking values in $\mathbb R^d$ and satisfies

\[ egin{aligned} dX_t = - abla V(X_t)dt + \sqrt{2}dW_t, \end{aligned}\]

where $B_t$ is the Brownian motion.

Then, we already have that $X_0 \sim ho_0$ is a random variable distributed according to $ ho_0$, then we calculate the infinitesimal generator of the Langevin Diffusion. Firstly, apply the Itô formula, we can rewrite the Langevin diffusion as:

\[ egin{aligned} f(X_t) - f(X_0) = \int_0^t -\langle abla f(X_s), abla V(X_s) angle + \mathrm{Tr}( abla^2 f(X_s))ds + \sqrt{2}\int_0^t \langle abla f(X_s), dW_s angle. \end{aligned}\]

Since $W_t$ is the Brownian motion in $\mathbb R^d$, hence $dW_t$ is mean-zero. Moreover, it is also independent from $X_t$ and $ abla f(X_t)$, then taking the expected value, we have

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E [\langle abla f(X_s), dW_s angle] = 0, \end{aligned}\]

or

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E \left[ \sqrt{2}\int_0^t\langle abla f(X_s), dW_s angle ight] = 0. \end{aligned}\]

Write down the remaining term as Taylor expansion, and take the expected value of both side, we also have

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E[f(X_t) | X_0 = x] - f(x) &= t[-\langle abla f(x), abla V(x) angle + \mathrm{Tr}( abla^2 f(x))] + o(t) \ rac{P_t f(x) - f(x)}{t}& = -\langle abla f(x), abla V(x) angle + \Delta f(x) + rac{o(t)}{t}, \end{aligned}\]

When $t o 0$, we have

\[ egin{aligned} Lf(x) = \lim_{t\searrow 0} rac{P_t f(x) - f(x)}{t} = -\langle abla f(x), abla V(x) angle + \Delta f(x). \end{aligned}\]

Moreover, from the chain rule, we also have

\[ egin{aligned} df(X_t) = Lf(X_t)dt + \sqrt{2} abla f(X_t) dW_t. \end{aligned}\]

Take the expectation of both sides, we have

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[f(X_t)] = \mathbb E[Lf(X_t)]. \end{aligned}\]

As $ ho_t$ has the law of $X_t$, then

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbb E[f(X_t)] = \int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x) ho_t(x)dx. \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt} \int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x) ho_t(x)dx &= \int_{\mathbb R^d} Lf(x) ho_t(x)dx \ &= \int_{\mathbb R^d} [\Delta f(x) -\langle abla f(x), abla V(x) angle ] ho_t(x)dx. \end{aligned}\]

From the divergence theorem, we imply that

\[ egin{aligned} abla f\cdot abla V ho_t = abla f \cdot ( ho_t abla V) = -f abla \cdot ( ho_t abla V), \end{aligned}\]

and we can rewrite as

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt}\int f ho_t = \int f (\Delta ho_t + abla \cdot ( ho_t abla V)). \end{aligned}\]

Using the definition of weak derivative, we imply that

\[ egin{aligned} \partial_t ho_t = \Delta ho_t + abla \cdot ( ho_t abla V) = \mathrm{div}(( abla \log ho_t + abla V) ho_t), \end{aligned}\]

where $\Delta$ denotes the Laplacian operator (diffusion) and the divergence operator as the drift, and the $\log ho_t$ is called the score of $ ho_t$. Furthermore, the continuity equation can also be described through a flow model on $\mathbb R^d$.
entry.summary: Summary of the derivation of the Langevin Diffusion
